confirmedMajors.issue: The 'marks failed only on terminal attempt' test feeds attemptsMade=2/attempts=3 as the terminal case and attemptsMade=0 as non-terminal, but the real Worker 'failed' event post-increments attemptsMade (values 1,2,3 for attempts=3), so this test locks in the premature-mark bug rather than exercising the true terminal (attemptsMade=3) and true penultimate (attemptsMade=2) cases.

verdict.reason: Confirmed via primary source (vendored bullmq 5.79). worker.js:662-663 emits the 'failed' event AFTER moveToFailed's attemptsMade+=1 (job.js:555), and retry lua persists the bump (retryJob-11.js:199, moveToDelayed-12.js:369, moveToFinished-14.js:977). Thus for attempts=3 the real failed-event attemptsMade sequence is 1,2,3: attemptsMade=2 is the penultimate failure with a retry still queued, attemptsMade=3 is the true terminal, and attemptsMade=0 never occurs. The processor's guard `attemptsMade + 1 >= maxAttempts` (pdf-export.processor.ts:76-78) therefore fires markExportFailed at attemptsMade=2 (penultimate, retry pending) — premature — as well as at 3, directly violating the test's stated contract 'only on the terminal attempt.' The test at line 375-421 feeds attemptsMade=2/attempts=3 as the case where markExportFailed MUST be called and attemptsMade=0 as the non-terminal case; since 0 is unreachable and 2 is the penultimate, the test locks in the premature-mark bug and never exercises the true terminal (3) or asserts the true penultimate (2) is skipped. The repo's own dlq-monitor.service.ts:132 uses the correct `attemptsMade >= attempts` (no +1) on the same post-incremented source, proving the processor's +1 is an off-by-one, not a deliberate documented choice; the email-reminder processor shares the identical bug and its test comments (lines 221,249) explicitly encode the mistaken 0-based model. Every refutation path (unreachable / deliberate / gated elsewhere) fails.

confirmedMajors.issue: The reorder test claims to prove composite keys track identity vs index keys, but a single server render always emits map() output in array order regardless of key strategy, so index keys would pass identically — the assertion cannot fail for its stated purpose.

verdict.reason: The finding is correct. react-email's `render` is static SSR (renderToReadableStream/StaticMarkup); the reorder test performs two independent fresh renders of [A,B] and [B,A]. In a fresh render, `Array.prototype.map` emits <li> in array order and React keys have no effect on static output order — keys only govern DOM-node reuse during reconciliation of an already-mounted tree across re-renders, which never occurs here. Concrete proof of the defect: substituting `key={index}` (or removing the key) in the template leaves all four assertions green (alicePosAB<bobPosAB and bobPosBA<alicePosAB are guaranteed purely by map ordering of the input arrays). Thus the test cannot fail for its stated purpose ("keys follow identity, not position") and provides zero protection for the composite-key invariant; its comment's premise that "index keys would still render in [A,B] order because React reconciles by position" is a misconception (position-reconciliation happens on re-render of a mounted tree, not on disjoint static renders). Not deliberate/documented (comment bakes in the wrong premise), not gated elsewhere (file avoids jsdom/RTL; the "same pair = same DOM node" reconciliation behavior is untestable via static SSR and covered nowhere), and the index-key-passes scenario is guaranteed reachable. Severity is modest (test-quality/false coverage, and the key distinction is practically moot for a write-once email), but the finding's substantive claim holds.

The finding's substantive assertion ("no regression in the actual formatter could ever trip it") is true but irrelevant — the test never claimed to guard the formatter; it restates a deliberate, documented design decision rather than identifying a defect. confirmedMajors.issue: The 'marks failed only on terminal attempt' test feeds attemptsMade=2/attempts=3 as the terminal case and attemptsMade=0 as non-terminal, but the real Worker 'failed' event post-increments attemptsMade (values 1,2,3 for attempts=3), so this test locks in the premature-mark bug rather than exercising the true terminal (attemptsMade=3) and true penultimate (attemptsMade=2) cases.

verdict.reason: Confirmed via primary source (vendored bullmq 5.79). worker.js:662-663 emits the 'failed' event AFTER moveToFailed's attemptsMade+=1 (job.js:555), and retry lua persists the bump (retryJob-11.js:199, moveToDelayed-12.js:369, moveToFinished-14.js:977). Thus for attempts=3 the real failed-event attemptsMade sequence is 1,2,3: attemptsMade=2 is the penultimate failure with a retry still queued, attemptsMade=3 is the true terminal, and attemptsMade=0 never occurs. The processor's guard `attemptsMade + 1 >= maxAttempts` (pdf-export.processor.ts:76-78) therefore fires markExportFailed at attemptsMade=2 (penultimate, retry pending) — premature — as well as at 3, directly violating the test's stated contract 'only on the terminal attempt.' The test at line 375-421 feeds attemptsMade=2/attempts=3 as the case where markExportFailed MUST be called and attemptsMade=0 as the non-terminal case; since 0 is unreachable and 2 is the penultimate, the test locks in the premature-mark bug and never exercises the true terminal (3) or asserts the true penultimate (2) is skipped. The repo's own dlq-monitor.service.ts:132 uses the correct `attemptsMade >= attempts` (no +1) on the same post-incremented source, proving the processor's +1 is an off-by-one, not a deliberate documented choice; the email-reminder processor shares the identical bug and its test comments (lines 221,249) explicitly encode the mistaken 0-based model. Every refutation path (unreachable / deliberate / gated elsewhere) fails.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. shutdownOtel (line 182) has zero callers anywhere: main.ts imports and calls only startOtel; the otel.bootstrap.test.ts imports only decideOtelBootstrap; a full-repo grep finds shutdownOtel only at its definition plus a stale dist/ artifact. startOtel already registers process.once SIGTERM/SIGINT (lines 176-177) with a local `shutdown` closure whose body is functionally identical to shutdownOtel, so it is a genuine duplicated, dead shutdown surface. It is not wired via NestJS enableShutdownHooks (the bootstrap is a standalone pre-Nest function, not a provider), not re-exported via any barrel, not listed in the module-public-api boundary fixture, not referenced by any openspec spec, and carries no doc/TODO/ComingSoon marker. The introducing commit (710b5534) documents decideOtelBootstrap's export rationale but is silent on shutdownOtel, and git log -S shows it has never had a caller since introduction — so this is not a deliberate documented decision. Concrete defect: an uncalled exported function duplicating the inline shutdown logic, and the two copies have already drifted (inline swallows errors and returns void; shutdownOtel returns the rejecting promise and does not deregister the signal handlers), making it a real maintainability/drift hazard rather than a drop-in replacement. Severity is low (dead code / tidiness), but the finding is accurate as stated.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, though latent (low severity). Verified facts: (1) userSessionSchema.userId is z.uuid() (packages/shared/src/schemas/auth.ts:74); (2) the constant PDF_EXPORT_SYNTHETIC_USER_ID = "a0000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000pdfwk" has group-5 "0000000pdfwk" containing non-hex chars p,d,f,w,k, so it provably fails z.uuid() (checked with a UUID regex). (3) The docblock at trpc.context.ts:31-38 explicitly states this synthetic session "must satisfy userSessionSchema (uuid userId, email, etc.)" — a direct, self-contradicting contract lie: the very constant the docblock documents cannot satisfy the schema it invokes. That contradiction is a real, present defect in the source, not speculation. Mitigating (why severity is low, not why it is refuted): the "would break" clause is conditional and does NOT fire today. I traced buildLegacyPdfExportSession (line 49): it returns the object directly, never calls hydrateSession, and is never re-parsed. The only userSessionSchema.parse calls (auth.controller.ts:43,55) are on the real-JWT sign/verify path the PDF-worker token never reaches. The legacy builder is also only reachable for pre-requestedBy tokens (shrinking 5-min back-compat window). So no runtime failure exists now — but the finding's articulable core defect (a docblock asserting a uuid contract that its own constant violates) is verified, so it cannot be refuted.

confirmedMajors.issue: isProcedureChainAllowed prefix-matches and PUBLIC_CHAIN=[metrics,logging] is a prefix of every protected chain, so some() short-circuits true for ANY procedure starting with the shared metrics+logging pair — the role middleware at slot 2 is never actually compared, so a hand-rolled role chain reusing metrics+logging passes the gate green, exactly the violation CLAUDE.md's role-coverage invariant forbids.

verdict.reason: CONFIRMED. isProcedureChainAllowed (role-coverage.test.ts:108-113) matches prefix-only: it guards `middlewares.length < chain.length` then compares just the first chain.length middlewares. PUBLIC_CHAIN is publicProcedure's chain = [metricsMiddleware, loggingMiddleware] (trpc.middleware.ts:356-358), length 2, and is index 0 in ALLOWED_CHAINS. Every protected chain is [metrics, logging, role, pdfExportGuard, mutationAudit], so PUBLIC_CHAIN is a genuine prefix of all of them. Therefore ALLOWED_CHAINS.some(...) short-circuits true on the 2-element public chain for ANY procedure whose first two middlewares are the shared metrics+logging refs — slot 2 (the role middleware) is never compared. The scenario is reachable and non-exotic: metricsMiddleware/loggingMiddleware are exported and publicProcedure itself IS [metrics, logging], so `publicProcedure.use(customRoleMw)` yields [metrics, logging, customRoleMw] and passes the gate green. This is exactly the hand-rolled chain CLAUDE.md's role-coverage invariant forbids ("must use one of the 9 canonical builders, matched by reference identity"). This test is the SOLE structural enforcement of that invariant (grep shows no complementary gate; other files reference role-coverage only as a fixture concern). The two mutation tests (lines 210-244) only exercise procedures built on a fresh initTRPC.create() with different middleware instances, so they never touch reuse of the real shared refs and mask the gap. The test's own doc comment (lines 32-39) claims slot 2 the role middleware is asserted against captured identities, but the code never checks it once the public prefix matches — the gate under-delivers vs both its comment and the stated invariant. Not documented as a deliberate narrowing. Concrete failure: a future procedure with a wrong/missing/buggy role guard but the shared metrics+logging prefix (e.g. publicProcedure.use(badRole), or protectedProcedure's prefix minus mutationAudit/pdfExportGuard) returns empty from findUncoveredProcedures and ships green.

verdict.reason: The finding is correct. react-email's `render` is static SSR (renderToReadableStream/StaticMarkup); the reorder test performs two independent fresh renders of [A,B] and [B,A]. In a fresh render, `Array.prototype.map` emits <li> in array order and React keys have no effect on static output order — keys only govern DOM-node reuse during reconciliation of an already-mounted tree across re-renders, which never occurs here. Concrete proof of the defect: substituting `key={index}` (or removing the key) in the template leaves all four assertions green (alicePosAB<bobPosAB and bobPosBA<alicePosAB are guaranteed purely by map ordering of the input arrays). Thus the test cannot fail for its stated purpose ("keys follow identity, not position") and provides zero protection for the composite-key invariant; its comment's premise that "index keys would still render in [A,B] order because React reconciles by position" is a misconception (position-reconciliation happens on re-render of a mounted tree, not on disjoint static renders). Not deliberate/documented (comment bakes in the wrong premise), not gated elsewhere (file avoids jsdom/RTL; the "same pair = same DOM node" reconciliation behavior is untestable via static SSR and covered nowhere), and the index-key-passes scenario is guaranteed reachable. Severity is modest (test-quality/false coverage, and the key distinction is practically moot for a write-once email), but the finding's substantive claim holds.

verdict.reason:
Claim CONFIRMED. `pdfExportRouter` + its two Context interfaces (`PdfExportRouterRequestContext`, `PdfExportRouterStatusContext`) in apps/api/src/modules/pdf-export/pdf-export.router.ts have exactly one importer in the whole repo: pdf-export.service.test.ts (line 19). No production code references them.

Concrete facts establishing dead production surface:
- The real, wired tRPC router is `createPdfExportRouter` in apps/api/src/infrastructure/trpc/routers/pdf-export.router.ts, imported by trpc.router.ts (line 39) and mounted. That production router does NOT import the module's `pdfExportRouter`; it builds its own `router({ request, status })` on `leadershipProcedure`, threads `ctx.session.role`, and maps domain errors via `mapDomainError`.
- The module barrel apps/api/src/modules/pdf-export/index.ts exports download-handler, module, and service only — it does NOT export pdf-export.router. So `pdfExportRouter` is not even reachable through the module's public surface.
- Grep across apps/packages/prisma shows zero non-test references to `pdfExportRouter`, `PdfExportRouterRequestContext`, or `PdfExportRouterStatusContext`.

Why it's a genuine defect, not a deliberate/documented choice:
- The file carries no comment, spec link, ADR, TODO, or ComingSoon marker justifying a second router object. The repo's own conventions ("Deferred features leave traces", "Exemplary by default", no dead code) are violated.
- The tests themselves label it a fixture: pdf-export.service.test.ts line 647 comment "Ensure router fixture forwards session userId to service" and line 648 "threads requestedBy from the router context". It is a plain adapter object (not a tRPC router) that exists solely so the test can call service methods through a context shape — i.e. a test fixture living in a production source file that gets compiled and shipped in the API bundle.
- It also gives false confidence: these two tests exercise the fixture, not the real production router (createPdfExportRouter), whose behavior differs (leadershipProcedure authz gate, role label threading, error mapping) and is completely untested by this describe block.

Concrete failure: the fixture object is compiled into the production API artifact yet is invoked by nothing at runtime; the request/status wiring the tests validate is a parallel re-implementation that diverges from the router actually mounted, so a regression in createPdfExportRouter (auth gate, role threading, error mapping) would not be caught by these passing "pdfExportRouter" tests. Correct home is the test file (or delete it and test createPdfExportRouter directly).

confirmedMajors.issue: getReportStatus is declared on the port and implemented by the Prisma adapter and every test stub, but no production code calls it (only its own doc comment references it) — dead surface every implementer must satisfy.

verdict.reason: Confirmed dead required surface. `getReportStatus` is declared as a REQUIRED (non-optional) method on the `ReportSectionsRepository` port (service.ts:68), implemented by the Prisma adapter with a real DB query (prisma-repository.ts:31-38) and by 4+ test stubs, yet no production code invokes it. Grep across all non-test .ts in apps/packages/prisma yields only the port declaration, one doc comment, and the adapter impl; grepping repository calls inside the service shows it uses getPublishedLineage, getReportMeta, getSectionById, getReportPeriodStatusForSection, saveSection, getMyHistoryRows — never getReportStatus. Refutation via the doc comment fails: service.ts:79-89 claims the service "falls back to getReportStatus" when getReportMeta is unimplemented, but evaluateDeadlineGate (lines 222-242) actually returns false in that case and never calls getReportStatus — the comment documents a fallback that does not exist, so the only documentation is stale/wrong rather than a deliberate decision. Test service.test.ts:294-300 even sets getReportStatus to a divergent value to prove the gate ignores it. Concrete defect: a mandatory port method with a real adapter query and cross-file stub burden that no production path exercises, kept alive only by an inaccurate comment left over from the migration to getReportMeta/getReportPeriodStatusForSection.

confirmedMajors.issue: The comment claims the service "falls back to getReportStatus and skips the late-flag computation" when getReportMeta is unimplemented, but evaluateDeadlineGate (line 224) simply returns false and never calls getReportStatus — the rationale misdescribes actual control flow and props up the dead method.

verdict.reason: Claim confirmed, not refuted. The getReportMeta? docstring (report-sections.service.ts:83-85) states the service "falls back to getReportStatus and skips the late-flag computation" when getReportMeta is unimplemented. But evaluateDeadlineGate (lines 222-225) short-circuits with `return false` and never references getReportStatus. grep across non-test source confirms getReportStatus has zero call sites: only the interface decl (line 68), this comment (line 84), and the unused prisma-repo impl (line 31). The service reads editability from getReportPeriodStatusForSection, never getReportStatus — service.test.ts:300 sets getReportStatus to "published" precisely to prove the gate ignores it. So getReportStatus is a dead port method and the comment describes a fallback code path that does not exist. Every factual assertion in the finding is verifiable and true; it is not speculative, not unreachable, and not a documented deliberate decision. Under this repo's explicit comment-hygiene / exemplary-code standard (comments must accurately describe current control flow, no narrating paths the code doesn't take), a comment that misdescribes control flow and serves as the sole stated rationale for dead code is a concrete, articulable defect.

files.summary: Solid high-precision rule set, but comment extraction has two heuristic gaps the sibling union gate already solved: it mis-reads `//` inside string literals as comments, and misses non-asterisk block-comment continuation lines.

findings.issue: commentPart uses indexOf("//"), so a `//` inside a string literal (e.g. a Jira URL "https://jira/PROJ-1234") is treated as a comment and the ticket-slug/phase rules can false-positive, wrongly blocking a legitimate commit.

A plain block comment whose continuation lines lack a leading `*` (e.g. `/*\n Phase 3 landed \n*/`) returns null and is never judged, so archaeology in non-JSDoc block comments evades the gate (confirmed: continuation line returns null).

files.summary: Careful SSOT gate: strips comments without eating `https://` in strings, preserves line numbers, handles union chains + z.enum + z.union(z.literal) idioms, realpaths both sides of the allowlist for the macOS /var symlink case, and exact-matches ReportStatus vs supersets per spec. No changes warranted.

Thorough behavioral coverage (16 passing): fires and non-fires for all four vocabularies, subsets/aliases/value-lists pass, comments and .d.ts/dist skip, backtick literal types, z.union non-literal members don't false-positive, `//`-in-string doesn't hide a union, and repo-rooted allowlist resolution incl. same-named-elsewhere. Assertions check exit status, per-file output, and hit counts, so they can genuinely fail.
